Before you start

Two accounts cover the whole product. Both use the password password.

Sign in atAccountWhat it shows
/login demo@cellaros.test Pro. One venue, three merchants, the full buying journey. This is the account you demo from.
/login group@cellaros.test Group. Two venues with their own merchants and a team. Show this second, and only briefly.
/login group.member@cellaros.test A team member who can only see the Riverside venue. Useful if someone asks about permissions.
/admin admin@cellaros.test The back office: suppliers, parsing, AI costs, and impersonating any account.
/supplier supplier@cellaros.test The supplier's own portal, where a merchant uploads their price list.

Putting the demo back

The walkthrough leaves things behind — a basket, a draft order, an approved price list. One command returns everything to the state described here:

$ php artisan demo:reset

It only touches the two demo companies and their five merchants. Real customers, real supplier catalogues and anyone else's data are left exactly as they were, so it is safe to run whenever you like — including straight after a demo, so the next one starts clean.

Run it before you start, too. If someone demoed yesterday, the basket and orders will still be theirs. Ten seconds now saves an awkward moment later.

The story to tell

The demo lands better as a story than a feature tour. The through-line:

A sommelier buys from several merchants. Their price lists arrive as spreadsheets and PDFs, all in different shapes. Right now that means a folder of files and a lot of memory. CellarOS reads those lists, puts every wine in one place, and tells you when you're about to pay more than you need to.

Everything below hangs off that sentence. If you only have five minutes, do steps 3, 4, 5 and 9 — the catalogue, the plain-English search, the price comparison, and repeating an order.

Sign in

Go to /login and sign in as demo@cellaros.test with the password password.

The dashboard

You land on the cellar overview: what the stock is worth, how many bottles and distinct wines are held, and how many wines are available to browse across the connected merchants.

Worth saying

"This is the bit a finance director asks for and a sommelier never has — what's actually sitting in the cellar, in money."

Two stock lines are deliberately low, so the low-stock alerts have something to point at. Scroll down to show the cellar composition by type and the recent orders.

The catalogue

Every wine from every merchant they buy from, in one table. Point out the columns — wine, producer, supplier, origin, grape, type, vintage, format, price.

Worth saying

"These came from three different merchants, in three different file formats. Nobody typed any of this in."

Use Columns to switch a couple off and on — the choice is remembered per person. Then use the supplier dropdown to filter to one merchant, and note that the supplier column disappears, because repeating it down every row would be noise.

Ask in plain English

In the box at the top, type something a person would actually say:

something fizzy and pink for a wedding, under £40

It takes a few seconds. What comes back is the important part: a sentence saying what it understood, the ordinary filters below filled in, and a line under each wine saying why it's there.

Worth saying

"It hasn't done anything mysterious — it's set the same filters you'd have set by hand. You can see exactly what it understood, and change any of it."

That is the point worth landing. It's not a black box that returns a list; it's a translator that hands you back a search you can audit and correct.

If someone asks something the catalogue can't express — "nothing from Bordeaux" — it says so plainly rather than guessing. Worth trying live if the room is sceptical.

Compare merchants on the same wine

Search for Malbec Estate and click the + on the first row.

The panel asks how many — bottles, or cases for a wine quoted by the case — and shows the line total as you go. Underneath, it lists the same wine from the other merchants they buy from, cheapest first, with the difference per bottle.

Worth saying

"Same wine, same vintage, same bottle — £2.40 a bottle cheaper from someone they already buy from. On twelve cases that's the software paying for itself."

Use this one switches the order to that merchant and keeps the quantity. Only merchants they're connected to are ever compared — nobody sees pricing from a merchant they don't trade with.

From basket to purchase orders

Add two or three wines from different merchants, then open the Basket. Adjust a quantity to show the totals move.

Click Create purchase orders. CellarOS splits the basket by merchant and raises one draft order for each — which is what actually has to happen, and what people currently do by hand.

Type and style

Open Filters and set Type to Sparkling. A Style filter appears alongside it: sparkling white, rosé, red, pét-nat.

Worth saying

"Filtering for sparkling always gives you the rosés too. The style only narrows it when you want it to — you never lose a wine by being more specific about it."

Fortified splits the same way — port, sherry, madeira, vermouth — which is the distinction anyone building a list actually needs.

Orders

Go to Orders. Three orders are waiting — a draft, one sent, one received — each with a proper PO number.

Open a row's actions menu. Everything an order can do lives there: download the PDF, email it to the merchant, receive it into inventory, repeat it.

Download the PDF if the room is interested — it's a real purchase order with the venue's details on it, ready to send.

Repeat an order

On the received order, choose Repeat this order.

You get a new draft with the same wines and quantities — and, at the top, a note about what has changed since last time. In the demo, two wines have moved in price.

Worth saying

"Same again is what a venue does every week. It re-prices from today's list rather than copying last month's, and tells you what moved — so nobody sends an order at a price that expired."

It reports wines that have become price-on-application, or that the merchant no longer lists, too. Nothing is dropped quietly; the buyer decides.

Inventory

Inventory is stock held at a venue. Each line carries the same detail as the catalogue — producer, merchant, origin, grape, type, vintage, format — alongside the count, the last price paid and when it arrived.

Nudge a quantity with the − and + buttons. Show Columns again: the same control, remembered separately from the catalogue's.

Suppliers

Suppliers lists the merchants this venue buys from. Open a row's actions menu: price lists and documents, importing a spreadsheet, allocating the merchant to particular venues.

A price list arrives

From Ashgrove Cellars' menu, choose Price lists & documents, then Review on the analysed list.

This is where a merchant's file becomes catalogue. On the left, how CellarOS read it — the column mapping it worked out, and how confident it is. Every wine it found is listed below for a human to approve, edit or reject, with anything suspicious flagged.

Worth saying

"It learned this merchant's format once. Their next list is read for free, in seconds, without anyone looking at it — and a person still signs off what reaches the catalogue."

Teaching it a merchant's words

On the review screen, look at the Wine types panel. Two words this merchant uses are highlighted because CellarOS couldn't place them: Skin Contact and Vin de Voile.

Set Skin Contact to Orange and save.

Worth saying

"Every merchant names things differently. You tell it once what a word means, and it uses that on everything they send from then on."

Worth adding: the words everyone agrees on are already known — crémant and pét-nat are sparkling, skin contact is orange wine — so this panel only ever holds a merchant's genuine house vocabulary.

The Group account

Sign out and back in as group@cellaros.test. Keep this short — two minutes at most.

  • There are two venues, switched with the selector on Inventory. Stock, orders and merchants are per venue.
  • Halliwell Fine Wine serves both venues; Saltmarsh Wine Co only serves Riverside. That's the allocation a group actually runs.
  • Team shows Leo Carter, a member scoped to Riverside only. Sign in as group.member@cellaros.test if anyone wants proof — he cannot see the HQ cellar or reach the Team page at all.
Worth saying

"Multiple venues is the difference between the two plans. Everything else is in both."

Admin and the supplier portal

Only show these if the conversation goes there — they're our side of the product, not the customer's.

The back office · /admin

  • Every supplier, their documents, and how each one is parsed — including whether re-reading their list is free or costs tokens.
  • AI costs: every billable call we've made, by model, with the running total. Useful if anyone asks what this costs to run.
  • Impersonate: view the app exactly as any customer sees it, with a banner and a one-click way back. The fastest way to answer "what does a customer actually see?"

The supplier's own portal · /supplier

Sign in as supplier@cellaros.test. Merchants get their own login to upload portfolios and price sheets — they never see buyers, prices or anyone else's data. One document is waiting to be analysed, one has been read, and one failed because it was a scan with no text in it.

Awkward questions, and honest answers

"Is the AI making up wines?"

No. The plain-English search only chooses filter values — it never writes a query and never invents a row. The reason under each wine is worked out from the criteria that wine actually meets, not written by the model, so it can't claim something that isn't true.

"What if it reads a price list wrong?"

Nothing reaches the catalogue without a person approving it. Rows that look wrong — a suspicious price, a missing one, a line that looks like a heading — are flagged, and bulk approval skips them.

"What does this cost to run?"

Most price lists are read by learned rules with no AI involved at all, so re-reading a merchant's next list is free. Where AI is needed it's logged per call in /admin/costs. The plain-English search runs on the cheapest model and costs a fraction of a penny per search.

"Where did these wines come from?"

The merchants in the demo are invented. The wine data is real — names, producers, regions and grapes taken from trade lists we've actually parsed — so the tables look like the trade rather than like test data. No real merchant's prices or relationships are shown.

"Can they see each other's prices?"

No. A buyer only ever sees the merchants they're connected to. The demo merchants are private to the demo accounts, which is why nothing here is visible to anyone else.

Commands

CommandWhat it does
php artisan demo:resetPuts the demo back to the state in this guide. Safe to run any time — only the demo accounts and their merchants are touched.
php artisan demo:reset --forceThe same, without the confirmation prompt.

If something looks wrong

  • The basket already has things in it — someone demoed before you. Run demo:reset.
  • The plain-English search returns nothing useful — it says what it understood; change a filter and carry on. If it can't reach the model at all it falls back to a plain text search and says so.
  • An order shows a wine as no longer listed — that's the feature working, not a bug. Say so.
